evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.232: quis haec nōn vel facile vel certē aliquō modō posset ēdiscere? (Lewis & Short)
Plaut. Stich. 4.2.41: exōrābō aliquō modō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The plain phrase: by some means, not said which.

terms.grammar: phrase used as a parenthesis, without changing the mood of the verb
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.146: fit enim, nesciō quōmodo, ut (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Sest. 100: bonī nesciō quōmodo tardiōrēs sunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Said in passing, as English says “somehow”, of what happens one cannot tell how (Lewis & Short, s.v. nesciō).

terms.gloss: somehow or other, by any means, however you can
evidence: Cic. Fam. 14.4.3: quōquō modō potes ad mē fac veniās
Cic. Q. fr. 1.2.4: tū quōquō modō hominem investīgēs velim (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of getting something done whatever it takes.
Its first sense is “somewhere, by some way”; in comedy, “in some way or other” (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Fin. 5.30: quōmodocumque dīcitur, intellegī tamen potest (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classically “in whatever way”, a relative adverb; for “somehow or other” aliquō modō is the classical phrase.

phrases.latin: tū mihi aliquid aliquō modō alicunde ab aliquibus blatīs
phrases.english: you babble something to me, somehow, from somewhere, from someone

phrases.latin: sī est spēs nostrī reditūs, eam cōnfīrmēs et rem adjuvēs; sīn, ut ego metuō, trānsāctum est, quōquō modō potes ad mē fac veniās.
phrases.english: if there is hope of my return, strengthen it and help the cause; but if, as I fear, it is all over, come to me somehow, however you can.
